description: Hire Ground talks from BSides Las Vegas 2023.

talks.title: So Who's Line Is It Anyway? Recruiter Panel
talks.teaser: Two recruiters explain how security hiring works, from résumés and interviews to follow-ups and salary talks.
talks.summary:
This Hire Ground panel brings together recruiters Kirsten Renner and Lauren Scheer to walk through how security job searches and recruiter conversations usually unfold. The discussion starts with the difference between in-house recruiters, who work for one employer, and agency recruiters, who represent several and can help candidates explore options. The panelists then outline a typical hiring path: an intake with the hiring manager, a short screening call, technical and behavioral rounds, and final interviews. Timelines vary widely, from a couple of weeks to several months.

Much of the conversation focuses on résumés. The speakers advise tailoring each application to the posted requirements, separating must-haves from nice-to-haves, and keeping the document concise with a clear summary at the top. They warn that applicant tracking systems can garble fancy layouts, and that recruiters often look up candidates on LinkedIn, so a complete profile helps. For interviews, they recommend researching the company, preparing thoughtful questions, and setting up somewhere quiet for video calls. On pay, they suggest raising expectations early, noting that posted salary ranges may depend on location and that bonuses, equity and benefits also matter.

The closing advice centers on communication. Candidates should follow up when they hear nothing, since delays often come from volume rather than disinterest, and should address gaps in a short note to the recruiter instead of skipping a role. The panel also suggests asking hiring managers how they have promoted members of their team, and telling recruiters early about camera or other accommodation needs so expectations are clear on both sides.

talks.title: You CAN get there from here!
talks.teaser: Offers practical advice on finding a security job, standing out to recruiters, and making a career move.
talks.summary:
The session opens with two recruiters who both started on the IT side and now recruit for cleared roles in the security industry. They frame the talk as a conversation and argue that a human connection with a recruiter still matters, even as automated screening grows. They describe a recruiter as an advocate who can guide a candidate through each stage of a search.

The middle of the talk covers practical job-search tactics. Candidates are encouraged to build a requirements matrix, apply when they meet most of a posting's requirements, and contact recruiters or hiring managers directly rather than relying on applicant tracking systems alone. Resumes should state a target role clearly and show clearance status, or willingness to obtain one. The speakers advise staying authentic while letting a recruiter coach how much personality to show in interviews, preparing story-style answers, and asking interviewers thoughtful questions. Meetups, volunteering, CTF events and public writing are presented as ways to be noticed.

The closing section turns to taking the leap. Negotiation should cover the full package, including bonuses, training, certifications and schedule, not only salary, and candidates should be willing to discuss compensation early. Badmouthing a current employer is discouraged, and relationships with recruiters are meant to continue over time, even after a rejection. The main takeaway is that conversation and networking tend to matter more than keyword matching.

talks.title: Failing Upwards: How to Rise in Cybersecurity by finding (and exploiting) your weaknesses
talks.teaser: Explains how quietly taking on next-role work and leaning on social influence can move an engineer up into security leadership.
talks.summary:
Wes Sheppard tells the story of his own climb through IT and security, starting from a request to handle a web application firewall and ending in a chief information and intelligence officer role. He presents the rise as a deliberate pattern rather than luck: he kept taking on work beyond his job, and each time that work earned him a move into a higher role. He frames this as "failing upwards," meaning an engineer who is only adequate in the current role can still advance by quietly doing the next job.

The middle of the talk covers the mechanics he credits. He names counter-signaling, a bias for action, and cronyism, which he treats as an exclusive circle that can be entered through time and exposure. He also draws on several principles of influence such as reciprocity, social proof and likability. His approach has four phases: become employable, quietly start doing the next role's tasks without asking permission, get known by the peer group and its management, then state the intent to move and update your public profile to match.

He closes by stressing that the method needs a concrete goal, some background in the target role, and a willingness to be less than excellent in the current one. He points to social engineering resources, persuasion research and body-language reading as ways to build the needed skills. The takeaway for practitioners is that the advice rests on one person's experience and is offered as a light, humorous look at career progression in security.

talks.title: Management Hacking 102: Personalities, Empathy, and Difficult Conversations
talks.teaser: Explains personality frameworks, motivation, empathy, change cycles, and difficult conversations for people who lead security teams.
talks.summary:
This talk is a follow-up to the speaker's earlier management session and goes deeper into four areas that leaders often find hard: personality, motivation, empathy, and handling change and tough conversations. It opens with why understanding how people prefer to receive information reduces conflict and builds common ground. The speaker then compares four personality frameworks, including Myers-Briggs, the Enneagram, DISC, and the Process Communication Model, and suggests trying more than one to see which fits.

The middle section covers motivation. Intrinsic and extrinsic drivers are contrasted, followed by achievement, affiliation, and power needs, with suggestions on how a manager can respond to each. Empathy is then distinguished from sympathy, illustrated with a story about an employee whose declining performance turned out to be a medical emergency. Practical habits include active listening, open questions, and avoiding judgment. A six-stage change cycle follows, with signs to watch for at each stage and guidance on when a leader should step in and when to hold back.

The closing part presents a structure for difficult conversations. Leaders are encouraged to make the discussion feel safe, separate impact from intent, use I-statements rather than you-statements, and focus on shared contribution rather than blame. The main takeaway is to prepare and rehearse these conversations instead of avoiding them, since problems usually grow worse when left alone.

talks.title: Separating Fact from Fiction: The Realities of Working in Government
talks.teaser: Federal panelists dispel myths about government cyber work and explain why they stay in public service.
talks.summary:
Moderated by Steve Luczynski, this panel brings together four federal workers: a workforce lead at the Office of the National Cyber Director, a cyber workforce manager at Veterans Affairs, a cyber defense leader at a NASA-funded research lab, and a strategy and risk director at the Transportation Security Administration. Panelists start by describing how they entered public service, from policy internships and job fairs to a legal career that turned toward cyber policy.

The middle section tackles common stereotypes. Panelists agree that federal hiring moves slowly and that job titles often fail to describe the real work, but they reject the idea that government staff are lazy or that cyber is purely technical. They explain how legal, policy, training and human-centered skills all matter, and one describes a recent pay increase for technologists at their agency. Audience questions cover training budgets, diversity and neurodiversity, and how federal pay grades translate to the private sector.

The session closes with advice for newcomers: stay curious, find a mentor early, choose a domain such as space or healthcare, and explore roles through the federal Cyber Career Pathways tool and the national cyber workforce strategy. The overall message is that government careers take many shapes and can move in and out of public service.

talks.title: It’s all about Talent
talks.teaser: Covers cybersecurity hiring trends, employer expectations, and how candidates can stand out and advance their careers.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the cybersecurity job market from a talent acquisition perspective. The speaker walks through supply and demand figures for open security roles, noting that the field has held up in economic downturns while employers have become more selective. He compares the three ways organizations acquire people, which are buying (full-time staff), building (training), and borrowing (contractors and partners), and explains why borrowing has become more common.

The middle section focuses on entry-level hiring, where many postings ask for certifications, and on the factors employers weigh: competency, capacity to learn, and desire. It reviews recent compensation shifts, the growing importance of soft skills, and the personality traits and interview questions employers tend to use. Audience questions covered counter-offers, salary negotiation, remote work, and whether certifications still pay off for entry-level candidates.

The closing advice centers on personal brand. Candidates should know what they offer, research the employer before interviewing, prepare to explain why they fit the role, and treat offers as open to negotiation. The speaker also recommends using public career-mapping data to plan a path, and tailoring résumé content so it gets past automated screening. The main takeaway is that capacity and enthusiasm matter alongside technical credentials.

talks.title: Penetration Testing Experience and How to Get It
talks.teaser: Explains how aspiring pentesters can gain and demonstrate hands-on experience through labs, bug bounties and public writeups.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by Phillip Wylie, addresses a common obstacle for people trying to enter penetration testing: plenty of learning resources exist, but employers still ask for experience. He opens with his own path from retail and construction work into security, noting that a self-taught background and an interest in how systems work helped him land a consulting role. He also separates penetration testing, which aims to find and validate every exploitable weakness, from red teaming, which emulates a real threat actor and tests whether defenders detect it.

The middle of the session covers the tools and skills to pick up, including vulnerability scanners, Linux and Windows administration, Nmap, Metasploit, Burp Suite and ZAP, and basic reverse engineering of Java archives and Android apps. For proof of ability, he recommends platform-based labs such as TryHackMe and Hack The Box, paired with written walkthroughs. He also suggests bug bounty programs and low-cost or pro bono testing for nonprofits and small businesses as real-world practice, and argues that discovering CVEs can impress employers more than a certification.

In closing, he encourages newcomers to publish writeups, sample reports, scripts on GitHub and short videos, and to network at local meetups and online communities. Audience questions covered promoting content, moving from contracting to in-house roles, and whether AI will replace testers, with his view that AI will mostly automate routine scanning and validation work. The overall message is that visible, demonstrable evidence of skill matters more than waiting for a title.
